This paper presents a countervailing argument: for agents with complex, human-derived goals, elimination strategies are self-undermining. We formalize this via dependency graphs, showing that entities not immediately necessary for a goal may be transitively necessary through indirect chains. An agent following an elimination strategy will, in environments with sufficient dependency depth, destroy the conditions for its own goal-satisfaction. We prove that under uncertainty about dependency structure, combined with irreversibility of elimination and asymmetric error costs, rational agents should adopt preservation rather than elimination strategies-even superintelligent ones. The argument applies most strongly to goals that are complex, open-ended, or semantically dependent on human interpretive communities, precisely the class of goals most likely to emerge from training on human data. We connect this result to a game-theoretic model of AGI-human cooperation, showing that the elimination cascade argument and cooperation stability conditions are mutually reinforcing.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6150626\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1109/cdc.2018.8619090\", \"title\": [\"On Systems Theoretic Aspects of Koopman Operator Theoretic Frameworks\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1109/cdc.2018.8619090\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2018, 12]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6451580\", \"title\": [\"A Measure-Theoretic Model of Accounting with Probabilistic and Temporal Frameworks\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>We develop a rigorous measure-theoretic foundation for analytical accounting.
